relations.subject: n1ql:group-by
relations.evidence: For more information and examples, see [GROUP BY Clause](../n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/groupby.md).

relations.subject: n1ql:group-by
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - a GROUP BY query's HAVING/LETTING clauses depend on an aggregate function having been named in the same query for their filter target to resolve
relations.evidence: To filter the groups by an aggregate function, use the HAVING clause within the GROUP BY clause.

notable_absence.finding: Consistent with groupby.json's own notable_absence (GROUP BY/HAVING/LETTING carry no privilege table of their own), this guide shows no privilege or role information anywhere - access control is asserted once at the keyspace/FROM level, not per aggregate/grouping clause.

cross_component_finding: REGISTRY DRIFT (not introduced here, flagging for reconciliation): two separate naming inconsistencies recur on this page's subject matter. (1) The reference page cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/aggregatefun.json minted the singular 'n1ql:aggregate-function' for the whole aggregate-function family, but cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/groupby.json independently minted a plural 'n1ql:aggregate-functions' as a seeAlso target for the identical page - this extraction used the singular, authoritative id. (2) The Grouping/Aggregate Pushdown concept exists under two ids: 'indexes:groupby-aggregate-performance' (minted in groupby.json as a seeAlso target) and 'index-type:group-aggregate-pushdown' (the actual concept minted directly from cloud/indexes/groupby-aggregate-performance.json) - this extraction used the latter, more authoritative id.
cross_product_finding: This guide adds no new domain concepts over the FILTER clause, aggregate quantifier (ALL/DISTINCT), GROUP BY, HAVING, and LETTING clauses already implicitly covered by n1ql:aggregate-function and n1ql:group-by in the round 5 sweep - it is entirely a worked-examples wrapper, confirming the batch's dominant pattern of guide-level content reusing statement-level vocabulary rather than revealing new structure.
